title: Similarity and Right-Triangle Trigonometry
bigQuestion: How can a triangle you can measure tell you the size of one you cannot reach?

story.title: The Flagpole and the Mirror
story.kicker: A class needs the height of a flagpole, and all they have is a tape measure, a small mirror and a little geometry.
paragraphs: The flagpole in front of a high school on the West Side of Chicago needed a new rope, and the hardware store wanted to know how much to cut. Nobody was going to climb it. Mr. Reyes's geometry class took the job. He handed Dani a tape measure and a small flat mirror and said, "You can find the height without leaving the ground."

Dani set the mirror flat on the sidewalk 10 meters from the base of the pole. Then she walked backward, away from the pole, keeping her eyes on the mirror. When she saw the top of the pole appear in the glass, she stopped. Marcus measured from the center of the mirror to the spot under her eyes: 2 meters. They also measured the height of her eyes above the ground: 1.6 meters.

Here is the trick. Light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it arrives. So the angle from the mirror up to Dani's eye equals the angle from the mirror up to the top of the pole. Both the pole and Dani stand straight up, so each makes a right angle with the ground. Two triangles share two equal angles, one at the mirror and one on the ground. That makes them the same shape, only different sizes.

Same shape means the sides come in the same ratio. Dani's eye height over her distance to the mirror must equal the pole's height over its distance to the mirror. So 1.6 ÷ 2 = 0.8, and the pole's height is 0.8 × 10 = 8 meters. The class checked it a second way: the pole's distance was 5 times Dani's, so its height was 5 × 1.6 = 8. The store cut 17 meters of rope, enough to go up, around the pulley and back down with a little to spare.

That idea, that a small triangle can stand in for a big one, is one of the oldest tools in mathematics. Surveyors use it to map land. Astronomers used it to find the distance to the Moon. This chapter builds the idea from the ground up, then turns the ratios of a right triangle into three tools called sine, cosine and tangent.
story.think: Dani could also have measured the flagpole's shadow instead of using a mirror. What would she need to measure, and why would that work?

lessons.title: Stretching From a Center
lessons.mainIdea: A dilation multiplies every distance from a center point by the same scale factor, so shapes keep their angles but change size.
reading: Zoom in on a photo on your phone. The picture gets bigger, but the people in it do not become fatter or taller in a strange way. Every part grows by the same amount. That is a *dilation*. A dilation has a *center* (the point that stays put) and a *scale factor*, a number that tells how much every distance from the center gets multiplied.

Try it with coordinates. Put the center at the origin (0, 0) and use scale factor 3. The point (2, 3) moves to (3 × 2, 3 × 3) = (6, 9). The point (−1, 4) moves to (−3, 12). Each new point sits on the same line through the origin as the old one, just 3 times farther out. If the scale factor is 1/2, the point (6, 9) moves to (3, 4.5), which is half as far from the center.

A scale factor greater than 1 makes an *enlargement*. A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes a *reduction*. A common mistake is to add the scale factor instead of multiplying: (2, 3) with scale factor 3 is not (5, 6). Another is to dilate only the x-coordinate. Both coordinates get multiplied.

Two things happen under any dilation. Every length in the shape is multiplied by the scale factor. Every angle stays exactly the same. A triangle with a 40° angle still has a 40° angle after you triple it. That second fact is the key to the whole chapter: dilations keep shape and change only size.

words.d: a transformation that multiplies every distance from a center point by the same scale factor
the fixed point of a dilation; it does not move
the number every length is multiplied by in a dilation; greater than 1 enlarges, between 0 and 1 shrinks
a dilation with scale factor greater than 1, which makes the figure bigger

look.title: The Print Shop
look.text: A print shop takes a 4 inch by 6 inch photo and enlarges it with scale factor 2.5. The new print is 2.5 × 4 = 10 inches by 2.5 × 6 = 15 inches. The corners are still right angles. The long side is still 1.5 times the short side, because 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 and 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
look.prompt: The shop also makes a wallet-size print with scale factor 0.5. What are its dimensions, and is the long side still 1.5 times the short side?

check.q: A dilation centered at the origin has scale factor 2.5. Where does the point (4, −2) land?
check.why: Multiply both coordinates by 2.5: 2.5 × 4 = 10 and 2.5 × (−2) = −5, so the image is (10, −5).

check.q: A segment 6 cm long is dilated with scale factor 1/3. How long is its image?
check.why: Lengths are multiplied by the scale factor: 6 × 1/3 = 2 cm. Dividing by 3, not subtracting 3, is the rule.

check.q: Which measurement of a triangle stays the same after a dilation with scale factor 4?
check.why: Dilations keep every angle the same. Side lengths and perimeter are multiplied by 4, and area is multiplied by 16.

lessons.title: What Similar Means
lessons.mainIdea: Two figures are similar when one is a dilation (plus slides, turns or flips) of the other: equal angles and proportional sides.
reading: A model of the Willis Tower on a shelf and the real tower on Wacker Drive have the same shape. Every angle on the model matches an angle on the tower, and every length on the model is the real length times the same tiny number. Figures like that are *similar*. Formally, two figures are similar if a dilation, possibly combined with a slide, a turn or a flip, carries one onto the other.

Check it with numbers. Triangle A has sides 3, 4 and 5. Triangle B has sides 6, 8 and 10. Pair up the *corresponding sides*, shortest with shortest and so on: 6/3 = 2, 8/4 = 2, 10/5 = 2. Every ratio is the same, so the sides are *proportional* and the scale factor from A to B is 2. Now look at triangle C with sides 6, 8 and 11. The ratios 2, 2 and 2.2 are not all equal, so C is not similar to A.

Perimeter and area scale differently. Triangle A has perimeter 12; triangle B has perimeter 24, twice as much. But the area of A is 1/2 × 3 × 4 = 6, and the area of B is 1/2 × 6 × 8 = 24, four times as much. Length is multiplied by the scale factor k. Area is multiplied by k², because area has two dimensions and each one is stretched. A common mistake is to double the area when the sides double.

words.d: having the same shape: equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides
sides that sit in matching positions in two figures, like the shortest side of each triangle
related by the same ratio; all pairs of corresponding sides give the same quotient

look.title: How Area Grows With the Scale Factor
look.cite: Computed from the rule new area = k² × original area
look.prompt: A blueprint is drawn at 1/20 of real size. If a room on the blueprint has area 3 square inches, what is the real area in square inches, and about how many square feet is that (144 square inches per square foot)?

check.q: A 4 by 6 rectangle and a 6 by 9 rectangle are similar. What is the scale factor from the small one to the large one?
check.why: Compare corresponding sides: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 and 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5. Both ratios agree, so the scale factor is 1.5.

check.q: Triangle P has sides 5, 7 and 9. Triangle Q has sides 10, 14 and 20. Are the triangles similar?
choices: Yes, because two of the sides doubled
It cannot be decided without the angles
check.why: The ratios are 10/5 = 2, 14/7 = 2, but 20/9 is about 2.22. The sides are not all in the same ratio, so the triangles are not similar.

check.q: Two similar triangles have scale factor 3. The smaller has area 8 square units. What is the area of the larger?
check.why: Area is multiplied by k² = 3² = 9, so 8 × 9 = 72. Multiplying by only 3 gives the perimeter rule, not the area rule.

lessons.title: Three Shortcuts for Triangles
lessons.mainIdea: You can prove two triangles similar with AA, SAS or SSS without checking all six parts.
reading: Checking three angles and three side ratios every time is slow. For triangles there are shortcuts. The most useful is *AA similarity*: if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar. Why does that work? The three angles of a triangle always add to 180°, so once two angles match, the third must match too, and the shapes are the same.

Try it. One triangle has angles 40° and 60°. Another has angles 60° and 80°. The first triangle's third angle is 180 − 40 − 60 = 80°. So the first has angles 40°, 60°, 80° and the second has 60°, 80° and 180 − 60 − 80 = 40°. Same three angles, so they are similar by AA, even though nobody told you a single side length.

Two more shortcuts use sides. *SAS similarity*: two pairs of sides are proportional and the angles between those sides are equal. A triangle with sides 4 and 6 around a 50° angle is similar to one with sides 6 and 9 around a 50° angle, because 6/4 = 1.5 and 9/6 = 1.5. *SSS similarity*: all three pairs of sides are proportional. Sides 2, 3, 4 and sides 4, 6, 8 give ratios 2, 2, 2, so those triangles are similar.

A common mistake with SAS is using an angle that is not between the two sides. The angle must be the one the two sides form. Another mistake is thinking AA needs the angles to be in the same order around the triangle. It does not; any two matching angles will do.

words.d: if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar
if two pairs of sides are proportional and the angles between them are equal, the triangles are similar
if all three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional, the triangles are similar

look.title: Two Ramps, One Angle
look.text: A loading ramp rises at an angle of 12° from the ground. A second, shorter ramp built for the same truck also rises at 12°. Both ramps meet the ground at 12° and stand on a vertical wall, so each forms a right triangle with a 12° angle and a 90° angle. That is two matching angles.
look.prompt: Which shortcut proves the two ramp triangles are similar? If the long ramp is 3 times the length of the short ramp, how do their heights compare?

check.q: Triangle 1 has angles 35° and 65°. Triangle 2 has angles 65° and 80°. Are they similar?
choices: Yes, by AA; the first triangle's third angle is 80°
No, because 35° is not in triangle 2
Only if their sides are also equal
check.why: Triangle 1's third angle is 180 − 35 − 65 = 80°, so both triangles have angles 35°, 65° and 80°. Two matching angles are enough: AA.

check.q: One triangle has sides 4 and 6 with a 50° angle between them. Another has sides 6 and 9 with a 50° angle between them. Which shortcut applies?
choices: AA, because both have a 50° angle
Not similar, because 50 is not a side
check.why: The ratios 6/4 = 1.5 and 9/6 = 1.5 match, and the included angles are both 50°. That is SAS similarity with scale factor 1.5.

check.q: Triangle R has sides 2, 3 and 4. Triangle S has sides 4, 6 and 8. Which statement is true?
choices: They are similar by SSS with scale factor 2
check.why: All three ratios equal 2: 4/2, 6/3 and 8/4. Proportional sides in all three pairs is SSS similarity. Subtracting sides is not the test.

lessons.title: A Line Parallel to One Side
lessons.mainIdea: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides into proportional pieces.
reading: Picture a triangle-shaped garden bed with one straight path cutting across it, parallel to the back edge. The path splits each of the two other edges into two pieces. Those pieces come in the same ratio on both edges. This is the *side-splitter rule*: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.

Here is why. Call the triangle ABC and let the parallel line meet side AB at D and side AC at E. Because DE is parallel to BC, the angle at D equals the angle at B (corresponding angles from parallel lines). Both triangles share angle A. So triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC by AA. Similar triangles have proportional sides, and a little algebra turns that into AD/DB = AE/EC.

Use it. Suppose AD = 4, DB = 6 and AE = 6. Set up 4/6 = 6/EC. Cross-multiply: 4 × EC = 36, so EC = 9. Check with the whole sides: AB = 10 and AC = 15, and 4/10 = 0.4 while 6/15 = 0.4. The pieces match. A common mistake is to compare a piece with the wrong whole, like 4/10 = 6/9. Keep pieces with pieces or wholes with wholes.

A special case: when D and E are *midpoints* of their sides, the segment DE is a *midsegment*. It is parallel to the third side and exactly half as long. If BC is 14, then DE is 7. Builders use this when they brace a triangular roof truss halfway up.

words.d: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides into proportional pieces
the point exactly halfway along a segment
a segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle; it is parallel to the third side and half as long

look.title: The Roof Truss
look.text: A triangular roof truss has a bottom beam 24 feet long. A carpenter adds a horizontal brace parallel to the bottom beam, attached one third of the way down each sloping side from the peak. The brace splits each sloping side into a top piece and a bottom piece in the ratio 1 to 2.
look.prompt: The small triangle above the brace is similar to the whole truss. What is the scale factor from the whole truss to the small triangle, and how long is the brace?

check.q: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 3, DB = 9 and AE = 2. Find EC.
check.why: Set up 3/9 = 2/EC. Cross-multiplying gives 3 × EC = 18, so EC = 6. Check: AD/AB = 3/12 = 1/4 and AE/AC = 2/8 = 1/4.

check.q: A midsegment of a triangle is parallel to a side of length 14. How long is the midsegment?
check.why: A midsegment is half the parallel side: 14 ÷ 2 = 7. Doubling gives 28, which is the mistake of going the wrong direction.

check.q: Why is triangle ADE similar to triangle ABC when DE is parallel to BC?
choices: Because DE is half of BC
Because both triangles are right triangles
Because parallel lines make equal corresponding angles and the triangles share angle A, so AA applies
check.why: The parallel lines give one pair of equal angles, and angle A belongs to both triangles. Two equal angles is AA similarity.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean Theorem, Proved
lessons.mainIdea: Dropping a perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse makes three similar triangles, and their proportions prove a² + b² = c².
reading: You have used a² + b² = c² since middle school. Similar triangles show why it is true. Start with a right triangle with legs a and b and *hypotenuse* c. From the right angle, draw the *altitude* straight down to the hypotenuse, hitting it at a right angle. The hypotenuse is now split into two pieces: d next to leg a, and e next to leg b, with d + e = c.

The altitude makes two small right triangles. Each small triangle shares an acute angle with the big one, and each has a right angle, so each is similar to the big triangle by AA. Compare the triangle containing leg a with the big triangle: a/c = d/a, which gives a² = c × d. Compare the other small triangle: b/c = e/b, so b² = c × e. Add them: a² + b² = c × d + c × e = c(d + e) = c × c = c².

Check it on a 6-8-10 triangle. Here a = 6, b = 8, c = 10. Then d = a²/c = 36/10 = 3.6 and e = b²/c = 64/10 = 6.4, and sure enough 3.6 + 6.4 = 10. The altitude itself satisfies h² = d × e = 3.6 × 6.4 = 23.04, so h = 4.8. A second route: the altitude equals ab/c = 48/10 = 4.8. Both routes agree.

The theorem also runs in reverse. If a triangle's sides satisfy a² + b² = c², it is a right triangle. Sides 5, 12, 13 work because 25 + 144 = 169. Sides 4, 5, 6 do not, since 16 + 25 = 41 and 36 ≠ 41, so that triangle has no right angle. A common mistake is adding the legs instead of their squares: 6 + 8 is not 10.

words.d: the longest side of a right triangle, across from the right angle
a segment from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side (or its extension)
in a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c²

look.title: Across the Grid
look.text: Chicago's streets form a grid. A delivery drone lifts off at a corner, and the drop-off point is 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north. A bike courier must ride 3 + 4 = 7 blocks along the streets. The drone flies the straight line, the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 and 4. That distance is √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 blocks.
look.prompt: A second delivery is 6 blocks east and 8 blocks north. How far does the drone fly, and how many blocks does the courier save by flying instead of riding?

check.q: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. How long is the hypotenuse?
check.why: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, and √169 = 13. Adding the legs (17) skips the squares; 169 is c², not c.

check.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 15 and one leg 9. How long is the other leg?
check.why: 15² − 9² = 225 − 81 = 144, and √144 = 12. Adding 225 + 81 = 306 gives about 17.5, the mistake of treating 9 and 15 as both legs.

check.q: In a 6-8-10 right triangle, how long is the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse?
check.why: The altitude equals (leg × leg) ÷ hypotenuse = 48 ÷ 10 = 4.8. Check: √(3.6 × 6.4) = √23.04 = 4.8. The values 3.6 and 6.4 are the pieces of the hypotenuse, not the altitude.

lessons.title: Two Triangles Worth Memorizing
lessons.mainIdea: In a 45-45-90 triangle the hypotenuse is leg × √2; in a 30-60-90 triangle the sides are x, x√3 and 2x.
reading: Cut a square along its diagonal and you get two *45-45-90 triangles*. Both legs are equal. If each leg is 1, the hypotenuse is √(1 + 1) = √2, about 1.414. Since every 45-45-90 triangle is similar to this one, the rule is: hypotenuse = leg × √2. A square tile 10 inches on a side has a diagonal of 10√2, about 14.1 inches.

Cut an equilateral triangle in half from a corner to the middle of the opposite side and you get a *30-60-90 triangle*. If the equilateral triangle has sides 2, the half-triangle has hypotenuse 2 and short leg 1 (half the base). The long leg is √(4 − 1) = √3, about 1.732. The rule: short leg x, hypotenuse 2x, long leg x√3. The short leg is always across from the 30° angle.

Try one. A 30-60-90 triangle has short leg 4. The hypotenuse is 2 × 4 = 8. The long leg is 4√3, about 6.93. Check with the Pythagorean theorem: 4² + (4√3)² = 16 + 48 = 64 = 8². Now go backward: if the hypotenuse is 12, the short leg is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 and the long leg is 6√3, about 10.4.

Common mistakes: putting √3 on the hypotenuse instead of the long leg, and forgetting that the short leg is across from the smallest angle. For a 45-45-90 triangle, if you know the hypotenuse, divide by √2 to get a leg: hypotenuse 10 gives legs of 10/√2 = 5√2, about 7.07.

words.d: a right triangle with two 45° angles; its legs are equal and its hypotenuse is leg × √2
a right triangle with 30° and 60° angles; sides are x (short leg), x√3 (long leg) and 2x (hypotenuse)
a triangle with all three sides equal and all three angles 60°

look.title: Long Leg of a 30-60-90 Triangle
look.cite: Computed from long leg = x√3 with √3 ≈ 1.732, rounded
look.prompt: Each long leg is what multiple of its short leg? What would the hypotenuse be in each row?

check.q: A 45-45-90 triangle has legs of 7. How long is the hypotenuse?
A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 12. How long is the long leg?
A 45-45-90 triangle has hypotenuse 10. How long is each leg?

lessons.title: Sine, Cosine and Tangent
lessons.mainIdea: For an acute angle in a right triangle, sine, cosine and tangent are side ratios that depend only on the angle, because all such triangles are similar.
reading: Every right triangle with a 30° angle is similar to every other one, by AA (they share 30° and 90°). Similar means proportional sides, so the ratio of any two sides is the same in all of them. That is a powerful fact. It means a ratio like (side across from 30°) ÷ (hypotenuse) is a fixed number that belongs to 30°, not to any one triangle. Ratios like this are the tools of *trigonometry*.

Pick an acute angle A in a right triangle. The side across from A is the *opposite* side. The leg next to A is the *adjacent* side. The longest side is the hypotenuse. Three ratios get names: *sine* of A = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, *cosine* of A = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, *tangent* of A = opposite ÷ adjacent. Many students remember them with SOH-CAH-TOA.

Work through a 3-4-5 triangle. Let angle A be across from the side of length 3. Then opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5. So sin A = 3/5 = 0.6, cos A = 4/5 = 0.8, tan A = 3/4 = 0.75. Now look at the other acute angle B, across from 4: sin B = 4/5 = 0.8, cos B = 3/5 = 0.6. The sine of one acute angle equals the cosine of the other, because A and B add to 90° and the opposite side of one is the adjacent side of the other.

A common mistake is labeling sides before choosing the angle. Which leg is opposite and which is adjacent changes when you switch angles. The hypotenuse never changes. Another mistake is writing a ratio bigger than 1 for sine or cosine; the hypotenuse is the longest side, so those two ratios are always less than 1.

words.d: the study of the relationships between the angles and sides of triangles
the side of a right triangle across from the angle you are working with
the leg of a right triangle next to the angle you are working with (not the hypotenuse)
for an acute angle of a right triangle, opposite side divided by hypotenuse
for an acute angle of a right triangle, adjacent side divided by hypotenuse

look.title: Sine of Some Common Angles
look.cite: Standard values; 45° and 60° are rounded to three decimal places
look.prompt: Why is sin 30° exactly 0.5? Think about the 30-60-90 triangle with short leg x and hypotenuse 2x. What is cos 60°, and why must it be the same number?

check.q: A right triangle has legs 8 and 15 and hypotenuse 17. What is the sine of the angle across from the side of length 8?
check.why: Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 8/17. The ratio 8/15 is the tangent, and 15/17 is the cosine.

check.q: In the same 8-15-17 triangle, what is the cosine of the angle across from the side of length 8?
check.why: Cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. The leg next to that angle is 15, so cos = 15/17.

check.q: Why is the sine of 30° the same number in every right triangle that has a 30° angle?
choices: Because all right triangles with a 30° angle are similar by AA, so their side ratios are equal
check.why: Any two right triangles with a 30° angle share two angles (30° and 90°), so they are similar and every ratio of corresponding sides is the same.

lessons.title: Finding a Missing Side
lessons.mainIdea: Choose the ratio that links the side you know, the side you want and the angle, then solve the equation.
reading: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall at a 70° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? Draw the right triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse (20 ft). The height is the side opposite the 70° angle. Opposite and hypotenuse means sine: sin 70° = height ÷ 20. A calculator gives sin 70° ≈ 0.940, so height = 20 × 0.940 = 18.8 feet.

The steps are always the same. First, mark the angle you know and label the two sides involved as opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse. Second, pick the ratio that uses exactly those two sides. Third, write the equation and solve. If the unknown is on top of the fraction, multiply. If it is on the bottom, divide.

Two more examples. A roof rises at 35° and the horizontal run is 50 feet. The rise is opposite, the run is adjacent, so tangent: tan 35° ≈ 0.700, and rise = 50 × 0.700 = 35.0 feet. Now suppose a zip line drops 12 meters and makes a 40° angle with the ground. The 12 m is opposite the angle and the cable is the hypotenuse, so sin 40° = 12 ÷ cable. Then cable = 12 ÷ sin 40° = 12 ÷ 0.643 ≈ 18.7 meters.

The most common mistake is choosing the wrong ratio, usually by mislabeling opposite and adjacent. Always label from the angle you are using. The second most common is multiplying when you should divide. When the unknown is the hypotenuse under a sine or cosine, you divide the known side by the ratio, and the answer must come out bigger than the known side.

words.d: for an acute angle of a right triangle, opposite side divided by adjacent side
find all the unknown sides and angles of a triangle from the parts you know
the vertical change of a ramp, roof or line
the horizontal change of a ramp, roof or line

look.title: The Kite Over the Lakefront
look.text: A kite flies over the lakefront with 50 meters of string let out. The string is straight and makes a 42° angle with the level ground. The string is the hypotenuse, and the kite's height is the side opposite the 42° angle. A calculator gives sin 42° ≈ 0.669.
look.prompt: How high is the kite? Then find how far the kite is from a point directly under the flier, using cos 42° ≈ 0.743.

check.q: A 30-foot ladder makes a 65° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? Use sin 65° ≈ 0.906.
check.why: Height is opposite the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so height = 30 × sin 65° = 30 × 0.906 = 27.2 ft. Dividing instead gives 33.1, which is impossible since it exceeds the ladder.

check.q: From a point 40 m from the base of a tree, the angle up to its top is 28°. How tall is the tree above eye level? Use tan 28° ≈ 0.532.
check.why: Height is opposite, 40 m is adjacent, so tangent: height = 40 × 0.532 = 21.3 m. Dividing 40 by 0.532 gives 75.2, the wrong direction.

check.q: A right triangle has a 50° angle whose opposite side is 15 cm. How long is the hypotenuse? Use sin 50° ≈ 0.766.
check.why: sin 50° = 15 ÷ hypotenuse, so hypotenuse = 15 ÷ 0.766 ≈ 19.6 cm. Multiplying gives 11.5, which is shorter than a leg and cannot be a hypotenuse.

lessons.title: Finding a Missing Angle
lessons.mainIdea: When you know two sides, form the ratio and use the inverse function (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹) to find the angle.
reading: Sometimes the sides are easy to measure and the angle is the mystery. Building codes under the Americans with Disabilities Act say a wheelchair ramp may rise at most 1 unit for every 12 units of run. What angle is that? The rise is opposite the angle and the run is adjacent, so tan θ = 1/12 ≈ 0.0833. To go from a ratio back to the angle, use the *inverse tangent*, written tan⁻¹. A calculator gives tan⁻¹(0.0833) ≈ 4.8°. A legal ramp is gentle.

The three inverse functions undo the three ratios. If sin θ = 0.6, then θ = sin⁻¹(0.6) ≈ 36.9°. If cos θ = 0.6, then θ = cos⁻¹(0.6) ≈ 53.1°. Notice these two add to 90°, which makes sense: in a 3-4-5 triangle, the angle with sine 0.6 and the angle with cosine 0.6 are the two acute angles. Once you find one acute angle, the other is 90° minus it.

Work an example. A roof rises 6 feet over a run of 9 feet. What is the roof's angle? tan θ = 6/9 ≈ 0.667, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.667) ≈ 33.7°. Check by going forward: tan 33.7° ≈ 0.667, and 9 × 0.667 ≈ 6. The other angle of the triangle is 90 − 33.7 = 56.3°.

A common mistake is typing sin⁻¹ when you built a tangent ratio; the inverse must match the ratio you formed. Another is writing 1/sin instead of sin⁻¹; the little −1 means "inverse function," not "reciprocal." And keep your calculator in degree mode, or the answer will come out in a different unit you will meet in the next chapter.

words.d: written tan⁻¹; the function that takes a tangent ratio and gives back the angle
written sin⁻¹; takes a sine ratio and returns the angle
a calculator setting that makes angle answers come out in degrees

look.title: Steep or Legal?
look.text: A school builds a ramp to a side door that sits 30 inches above the sidewalk. The ramp runs 300 inches along the ground. Its slope ratio is 30/300 = 0.1, so tan θ = 0.1 and θ = tan⁻¹(0.1) ≈ 5.7°. The rule of thumb for an accessible ramp is 1 to 12, which is tan⁻¹(1/12) ≈ 4.8°.
look.prompt: Is this ramp within the 1 to 12 rule? What is the shortest run that would make it legal for a 30 inch rise?

check.q: A right triangle has legs of 5 and 5. What is each acute angle?
check.why: tan θ = 5/5 = 1, and tan⁻¹(1) = 45°. Equal legs always give two 45° angles.

check.q: For an acute angle θ in a right triangle, sin θ = 0.5. What is θ?
check.why: sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°, the 30-60-90 fact: the short leg is half the hypotenuse. 60° is the angle whose cosine is 0.5.

check.q: In a right triangle, one acute angle has cos θ = 0.6, and cos⁻¹(0.6) ≈ 53.1°. What is the other acute angle?
check.why: The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, so the other is 90 − 53.1 = 36.9°. Subtracting from 180 forgets the right angle.

lessons.title: Looking Up and Looking Down
lessons.mainIdea: The angle of elevation looks up from horizontal and the angle of depression looks down; between two points they are equal.
reading: Stand on the lakefront and look up at the top of a skyscraper. Your line of sight tilts up from the horizontal. That tilt is the *angle of elevation*. Now imagine standing on the roof looking down at a boat. Your line of sight tilts down from horizontal. That is the *angle of depression*. Because the ground and the horizontal line from the roof are parallel, the angle of depression from the roof equals the angle of elevation from the boat. They are alternate interior angles.

Elevation example. You stand 40 meters from a building, and your eyes are 1.5 meters above the ground. The angle of elevation to the roof is 60°. The height above your eyes is opposite the angle and 40 m is adjacent, so use tangent: height = 40 × tan 60° = 40 × 1.732 = 69.3 m. Add your eye height: 69.3 + 1.5 = 70.8 m. Forgetting the eye height is the most common mistake here.

Depression example. A lighthouse keeper 100 meters above the water sees a boat at an angle of depression of 20°. The angle of elevation from the boat is also 20°. From the boat, the 100 m tower is opposite and the distance across the water is adjacent, so tan 20° = 100 ÷ distance. Then distance = 100 ÷ tan 20° = 100 ÷ 0.364 ≈ 274.7 meters.

A drawing error causes more wrong answers than arithmetic does. The angle of depression is measured from the horizontal line at the top, not from the vertical wall. If you put the 20° next to the tower instead of next to the horizontal, you will solve for the wrong side. Draw the horizontal line first, then the angle.

words.d: the angle between the horizontal and a line of sight looking upward
the angle between the horizontal and a line of sight looking downward
angles on opposite sides of a transversal, between two parallel lines; they are equal
the straight line from an observer's eye to the object being viewed

look.title: Sizing Up the Willis Tower
look.text: The roof of the Willis Tower stands about 1,450 feet above the street. Suppose you stand on the sidewalk 1,000 feet from its base and sight the roof. The tower is opposite your angle and the 1,000 feet is adjacent, so tan θ = 1450/1000 = 1.45. A calculator gives tan⁻¹(1.45) ≈ 55.4°.
look.prompt: If you walked back until you were 2,000 feet away, would the angle of elevation be half as big? Compute it with tan⁻¹(0.725) ≈ 35.9° and explain.

check.q: From a point 60 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 35°. How high is the top above eye level? Use tan 35° ≈ 0.700.
check.why: The height is opposite and 60 m is adjacent: height = 60 × 0.700 = 42 m. Dividing gives 85.7, and 34.4 comes from using sine by mistake.

check.q: From the top of an 80 m cliff, the angle of depression to a boat is 25°. How far is the boat from the base of the cliff? Use tan 25° ≈ 0.466.
check.why: The angle of elevation from the boat is also 25°. tan 25° = 80 ÷ distance, so distance = 80 ÷ 0.466 ≈ 171.7 m. Multiplying gives 37.3, which would put the boat closer than the cliff is tall.

check.q: Why does the angle of depression from a tower to a car equal the angle of elevation from the car to the tower?
choices: Because the horizontal lines at the top and at the ground are parallel, making the two angles alternate interior angles
Because sine and cosine are equal
check.why: The line of sight is a transversal crossing two parallel horizontal lines. Alternate interior angles on a transversal are equal.

lessons.title: Shadows, Mirrors and Rivers
lessons.mainIdea: Indirect measurement uses a small triangle you can measure and a similar large one you cannot.
reading: The oldest trick in surveying is the *shadow method*. On a sunny afternoon, a 1.8-meter-tall person casts a 2.4-meter shadow. At the same moment, a nearby tree casts a 12-meter shadow. The Sun's rays are parallel, so both triangles have the same angle at the tip of the shadow, and both have a right angle at the ground. AA similarity again. Then tree height ÷ 12 = 1.8 ÷ 2.4, and the tree is 12 × 1.8 ÷ 2.4 = 12 × 0.75 = 9 meters tall. Measure both shadows at the same time; a few minutes later the Sun has moved.

The *mirror method* from the chapter story works when the Sun is not out. A mirror on the ground reflects light at the same angle it arrives, so the triangle from your eye to the mirror and the triangle from the object's top to the mirror share an angle at the mirror and a right angle at the ground. With eye height 1.6 m, 2.5 m from you to the mirror and 30 m from the mirror to a building, the building's height is 1.6 × 30 ÷ 2.5 = 19.2 m.

You can measure across a river the same way. Stand directly across from a tree on the far bank. Walk 40 m along your bank and drive in a stake. Walk 10 m farther. Then turn and walk straight away from the river until the stake lines up with the tree; say that takes 8 m. The small triangle (10 by 8) is similar to the big one (40 by the river's width). River width = 40 × 8 ÷ 10 = 32 m.

Every method rests on the same two facts: two triangles with two matching angles are similar, and similar triangles have proportional sides. The common mistake is pairing sides that do not correspond, like the person's height with the tree's shadow. Write the proportion as height over shadow for both, or small over big for both, and keep it consistent.

words.d: finding a length you cannot measure directly by using a similar triangle you can measure
using the shadows of an object and a known height, cast at the same time, to find the object's height
using a mirror on the ground and the equal angles of reflection to form two similar triangles

look.title: Thales and the Pyramid
look.text: A story told since ancient times says the Greek thinker Thales found the height of a pyramid in Egypt by measuring its shadow. He waited until his own shadow was exactly as long as he was tall. At that moment the Sun's rays hit at 45°, so every object's shadow equaled its height. Then the pyramid's shadow, measured from the center of its base, gave its height directly.
look.prompt: Why did waiting for that moment make the math easier? If Thales had measured when his 1.7 m body cast a 3.4 m shadow, what would he multiply the pyramid's shadow by?

check.q: A 1.5 m person casts a 2 m shadow. At the same time a pole casts a 10 m shadow. How tall is the pole?
check.why: Height ÷ shadow is the same for both: 1.5/2 = 0.75, so the pole is 10 × 0.75 = 7.5 m. Using 2/1.5 instead gives 13.3, a flipped ratio.

check.q: Your eyes are 1.6 m high. You stand 2.5 m from a mirror on the ground, and the mirror is 30 m from a building whose top you see in it. How tall is the building?
check.why: Building ÷ 30 = 1.6 ÷ 2.5 = 0.64, so the building is 30 × 0.64 = 19.2 m. Forgetting to divide by 2.5 gives 48.

check.q: What fact makes the mirror method produce similar triangles?
choices: Light reflects off the mirror at the same angle it arrives, giving equal angles at the mirror
The observer must be exactly half the height of the object
The mirror must be a perfect circle
check.why: Equal angles at the mirror plus right angles at the ground give two matching angles, so the triangles are similar by AA.

review.q: A segment of length 2.5 is dilated with scale factor 4. How long is the image?
review.why: Multiply the length by the scale factor: 2.5 × 4 = 10. Adding 4 gives 6.5, the wrong operation.

review.q: One triangle has angles 50° and 70°. Another has angles 60° and 70°. Are they similar?
choices: Yes, by AA, since the first triangle's third angle is 60°
review.why: 180 − 50 − 70 = 60°, so the first triangle also has a 60° angle. Two shared angles (60° and 70°) is AA.

review.q: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC. AD = 6, DB = 4 and AE = 9. Find EC.
review.why: 6/4 = 9/EC, so 6 × EC = 36 and EC = 6. Check: AD/AB = 6/10 and AE/AC = 9/15, both 0.6.

review.q: A right triangle has legs 7 and 24. How long is the hypotenuse?
review.why: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625, and √625 = 25. Adding the legs gives 31; 625 is the square of the answer.

review.q: A 30-60-90 triangle has short leg 5. How long is the hypotenuse?
review.why: In a 30-60-90 triangle the hypotenuse is twice the short leg: 2 × 5 = 10. The value 5√3 is the long leg.

review.q: In a 5-12-13 right triangle, what is the tangent of the angle across from the side of length 12?
review.why: Tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent = 12/5 = 2.4. The ratio 12/13 is the sine of that angle.

review.q: A right triangle has a 50° angle and hypotenuse 20. How long is the leg adjacent to the 50° angle? Use cos 50° ≈ 0.643.
review.why: Adjacent = hypotenuse × cos 50° = 20 × 0.643 ≈ 12.9. The value 15.3 is the opposite leg (20 × sin 50°).

review.q: A 2 m stick casts a 3 m shadow while a building casts a 27 m shadow. How tall is the building?
review.why: Height ÷ shadow = 2/3 for both, so the building is 27 × 2/3 = 18 m. Using 3/2 instead gives 40.5.
